q: A condition that increases the probability of a loss, such as poor housekeeping in a factory, is called a(n):
explain: A hazard is a condition that increases the chance of loss; a peril is the cause of loss itself (fire, windstorm), and exposure is the state of being subject to loss.
source: IRMI glossary: hazard; peril; exposure

q: A contractor decides to stop accepting asbestos-removal jobs because of the liability involved. Which method of handling risk is this?
explain: Avoidance prevents the risk entirely by not engaging in the activity that creates it. Reduction would lower frequency or severity while still doing the work.
source: IRMI glossary: avoidance

q: A warehouse owner installs an automatic sprinkler system to limit the size of any fire. This is an example of:
explain: Loss reduction focuses on lowering the severity of losses that do occur; sprinklers and firewalls are classic examples.
source: IRMI glossary: loss control; loss reduction

q: All of the following are characteristics of an ideally insurable risk EXCEPT:
choices: There should be a large number of similar exposure units
The loss should be accidental and unintentional
The premium should be economically feasible
The potential loss should be catastrophic
explain: An ideally insurable risk should NOT produce catastrophic loss, because many units suffering loss at once defeats risk pooling. The other three are standard characteristics.
source: Rejda & McNamara, Principles of Risk Management and Insurance (13th ed.), Characteristics of an Ideally Insurable Risk

q: The tendency of people who believe they have a higher-than-average chance of loss to seek insurance more often than others is called:
explain: Adverse selection is the imbalance created when high-risk persons buy insurance to a much greater degree than low-risk persons; underwriting tries to counter it.
source: IRMI glossary: adverse selection

q: According to the law of large numbers, as the number of independent exposure units in a group increases:
choices: The probability that any single unit will suffer a loss decreases
Actual losses become more likely to approximate expected losses
Premiums must increase to pay for catastrophic losses
explain: The law of large numbers says larger pools make actual results more predictable (closer to expected); it does not change any one unit's own chance of loss.
source: IRMI glossary: law of large numbers

q: An insurer separately negotiates reinsurance on one large office tower, and the reinsurer is free to accept or decline that particular risk. This is:
explain: Facultative reinsurance is negotiated risk by risk, and the reinsurer may decline any submission. Under a treaty, the reinsurer must accept all business that falls within the treaty.
source: IRMI glossary: facultative reinsurance; treaty reinsurance

q: Under a quota share reinsurance agreement, the reinsurer:
choices: Pays only the portion of a loss that exceeds the ceding company's retention
Reviews and accepts or rejects each risk individually
Pays losses only after an annual aggregate deductible is met
Receives a set percentage of premiums and pays that percentage of losses
explain: Pro rata (proportional) reinsurance shares premium and losses in the same fixed percentage; quota share cedes an agreed percentage of every risk in a class. Paying only above a retention describes excess of loss.
source: IRMI glossary: quota share reinsurance; pro rata reinsurance; excess of loss reinsurance

q: An unincorporated group of subscribers that pool their risks and are managed by an attorney-in-fact is a:
explain: A reciprocal (interinsurance exchange) is an unincorporated group of subscribers managed by an attorney-in-fact. A stock company is owned by stockholders.
source: IRMI glossary: reciprocal; stock company

q: Under A.M. Best's Financial Strength Rating scale, ratings of A and A- carry which descriptor?
explain: A.M. Best: A++/A+ = Superior; A/A- = Excellent; B++/B+ = Good; B/B- = Fair.
source: A.M. Best, Guide to Best's Financial Strength Ratings

q: Under the independent agency (American agency) system, who owns the policy records and expiration data?
explain: In the independent agency system the agent retains ownership, use, and control of policy records and expirations; this distinguishes it from exclusive-agency and direct-writer systems.
source: IRMI glossary: independent agency system

q: An insurer ends an agent's binding authority but leaves the agent with its signage and blank binder forms. A customer who reasonably believes the agent can still bind coverage obtains a binder. The agent's authority to bind in this situation is best described as:
explain: Apparent authority is the power a reasonable person would believe the agent has based on the principal's conduct; the insurer may be estopped from denying it. Express authority is what the agency contract actually grants, and here it had been withdrawn.
source: IRMI glossary: apparent agency; express authority

q: Under the Michigan Insurance Code, a licensed producer who is not appointed by the insurer with which a policy is placed is treated as:
choices: A subagent of the insurer's appointed producer
explain: MCL 500.1201(b) defines an 'agent of the insured' as a producer not appointed by the placing insurer and treats that producer as representing the insured, not the insurer.

q: Under Michigan law, premiums an agent receives from customers must be:
choices: Deposited in the agency's operating account until the end of the month
Treated as fiduciary money and segregated from the agent's own funds
Held until the policy is issued, with any return premium retained by the agent
explain: An agent is a fiduciary for money received as agent and must segregate premiums and return premiums from the agent's own money. Failing to remit on time is prima facie evidence of a fiduciary violation.

q: In an insurance contract, the insured's consideration consists of:
choices: The insurer's promise to pay covered losses under the policy
The producer's signature on the completed application
Payment of premium and compliance with policy provisions
explain: The homeowners policy states the insurer provides coverage 'in return for the premium and compliance with all applicable provisions of this policy.' The promise to pay is the insurer's consideration.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Agreement; NCCI WC 00 00 00 C preamble

sub: Distinct Characteristics of an Insurance Contract
q: An insured pays one month's premium and then has a $300,000 covered fire loss. This unequal exchange of value, which depends on an uncertain event, shows that an insurance policy is a(n):
explain: An aleatory contract involves an uncertain event and an unequal transfer of value. Adhesion refers to the take-it-or-leave-it drafting, and unilateral means only the insurer makes an enforceable promise.
source: IRMI glossary: aleatory contract

q: Because an insurance policy is a contract of adhesion, courts generally resolve a genuine ambiguity in the policy wording:
choices: Against the insurer that drafted the policy
According to the producer's oral explanation
By striking the ambiguous provision from the policy
explain: Contracts of adhesion are offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, so courts construe ambiguities against the drafter. Michigan's Supreme Court reaffirmed this rule in Wilkie (2003).
source: IRMI glossary: contract of adhesion; Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003)

q: An applicant knows a material fact that would affect the insurer's decision but intentionally says nothing about it because the application did not ask. This is:
explain: Concealment is the willful withholding of pertinent information even though the insured was not asked about it, and it can void the policy. A misrepresentation is an affirmatively false statement.
source: IRMI glossary: concealment; ISO CP 00 90 07 88, A

q: An insurer has accepted an insured's late premium payments for several years and then tries to cancel the policy because a payment was late. The doctrine that may prevent the cancellation is:
explain: Estoppel prevents a party from contradicting its own prior conduct when another party reasonably relied on it; repeatedly accepting late payments is IRMI's own example.
source: IRMI glossary: estoppel

q: Some courts interpret a policy to provide the coverage an insured would reasonably have expected, even if the policy wording does not provide it. This is the:
explain: This is the reasonable expectations doctrine. Note that Michigan's Supreme Court (Wilkie, 2003) declined to adopt it and enforces unambiguous policies as written.
source: IRMI glossary: reasonable expectations doctrine; Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003)

q: For property insurance, when must the insured have an insurable interest in order to collect for a loss?
choices: Only at the time the policy is issued
At policy inception and each renewal, but not necessarily at the time of loss
At the time of the loss
explain: Property policies pay an insured no more than that insured's interest at the time of loss; the ISO BPP likewise limits payment to the insured's financial interest.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. A; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.4.d

q: An insurer's book of business has earned premiums of $2,000,000 and incurred losses of $1,300,000. What is the loss ratio?
explain: Loss ratio = incurred losses / earned premiums = $1,300,000 / $2,000,000 = 65%.
source: IRMI glossary: loss ratio

q: A store owner stops locking the back door at night because 'insurance will pay if anything is stolen.' This is an example of a:
explain: A morale hazard is indifference to loss because insurance will pay. A moral hazard arises from the insured's character, such as dishonesty.
source: IRMI glossary: morale hazard; moral hazard

sub: Negligence - Elements of a Negligent Act
q: All of the following are elements a plaintiff must prove to establish negligence EXCEPT:
choices: The defendant owed the plaintiff a legal duty
The breach was the proximate cause of actual injury or damage
The defendant intended to cause harm
explain: Negligence requires a duty, a breach, proximate cause, and actual damage; intent is not an element (intentional harm is a different tort).
source: IRMI glossary: negligence

q: Under Michigan's general comparative fault statute, a plaintiff found 60% at fault for her own injuries:
choices: May recover economic damages reduced by 60%, but no noneconomic damages
Is barred from recovering any damages
May recover all damages, including noneconomic damages, reduced by 60%
May recover full damages, with no reduction for her own fault
explain: MCL 600.2959 reduces damages by the plaintiff's percentage of fault. If the plaintiff's fault is greater than the combined fault of the others, economic damages are reduced and noneconomic damages are not awarded.

q: In a Michigan negligence suit, the plaintiff proves $100,000 of economic damages and is found 30% at fault. The plaintiff can recover:
explain: Contributory fault does not bar recovery in Michigan; damages are reduced by the plaintiff's 30% share ($100,000 - $30,000 = $70,000).

q: Under Michigan law, punitive damages are generally:
choices: Available in any negligence case at the jury's discretion
Capped at three times compensatory damages
Not recoverable unless expressly authorized by statute
explain: Michigan courts hold punitive damages are available only when expressly authorized by the Legislature. Michigan 'exemplary' damages are compensatory in nature.
source: Gilbert v DaimlerChrysler Corp, 685 NW2d 391 (Mich 2004); Casey v Auto Owners Ins Co, 729 NW2d 277 (Mich App 2006) (via IADC Michigan Damages Compendium)

q: A delivery driver negligently injures a pedestrian while making deliveries for his employer, and the employer is held legally responsible. The employer's liability is:
explain: Vicarious liability makes a principal (here, the employer) liable for the acts of its agents or employees, under the doctrine of respondeat superior.
source: IRMI glossary: vicarious liability; LII Wex: vicarious liability

q: A demolition company using explosives is held liable for damage to nearby buildings even though it used every reasonable precaution. This is an example of:
explain: Ultrahazardous activities such as blasting create liability without regard to fault; using due care is not a defense.
source: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§519-520; LII Wex: strict liability (abnormally dangerous activities)

q: Under a special (open) perils property policy:
choices: Only the perils specifically listed in the policy are covered
Direct physical loss is covered unless specifically excluded
The insured must prove a listed peril caused the loss
Only fire and lightning are covered unless the policy is endorsed
explain: Open (special) perils coverage insures against all causes of loss except those specifically excluded. Named perils covers only the listed perils.
source: IRMI glossary: open perils; special perils; named perils coverage

q: A fire damages an apartment building. Which of the following is a consequential (indirect) loss?
choices: Smoke damage to the interior walls
The cost to replace the burned roof
Rental income lost while the building is being repaired
Water damage to carpets from the fire department's hoses
explain: A consequential loss results from direct damage (for example, loss of rent). The other choices are direct physical damage to the property.
source: IRMI glossary: consequential loss; direct loss

q: A single limit of insurance that applies to both the building and business personal property at two locations is:
explain: Blanket insurance covers two or more items under one limit; specific insurance gives each item its own separate limit.
source: ISO CP 03 21 10 12 (definitions of specific and blanket insurance); IRMI glossary: blanket limit

q: Which of ISO's six commercial construction classes is the most fire-resistive?
explain: ISO codes run from 1 (frame, least fire-resistive) to 6 (fire resistive: walls, floors, and roof rated at least 2 hours).
source: IRMI glossary: fire resistive construction; modified fire resistive construction; joisted masonry construction

q: A 10-year-old roof would cost $20,000 to replace today and has depreciated 40%. Using replacement cost minus depreciation, the roof's actual cash value is:
explain: ACV = replacement cost - depreciation = $20,000 - (40% x $20,000) = $12,000. $8,000 is the depreciation amount, not the ACV.
source: IRMI glossary: actual cash value

q: The Agreed Value optional coverage in the Building and Personal Property Coverage Form:
choices: Replaces actual cash value with replacement cost
Increases the limit by a stated annual percentage
explain: Agreed Value removes the Coinsurance condition until the agreed value expiration date. Replacement Cost and Inflation Guard are separate optional coverages.

q: Which part of a policy identifies the named insured, the policy period, the insured location, and the limits?
explain: The declarations page shows the key information that varies from insured to insured. The insuring agreement states the insurer's promise to pay.
source: IRMI glossary: declarations; insuring agreement

q: A building is insured under Policy A for $300,000 and Policy B for $200,000. Both are written on the same basis with pro rata other-insurance clauses. A $100,000 covered loss occurs. How much does Policy B pay?
explain: Each insurer pays the proportion its limit bears to all limits: $200,000 / $500,000 = 40%, and 40% x $100,000 = $40,000. Policy A pays $60,000.
source: ISO CP 00 90 07 88, G.1; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. G

sub: Other Insurance - Contribution by Equal Shares
q: Two CGL policies apply to a $250,000 covered claim, and both permit contribution by equal shares. Policy A has a $100,000 limit and Policy B has a $300,000 limit. How much does Policy B pay?
explain: Under equal shares, each insurer pays equally until its limit is used up: A and B each pay $100,000 (A is exhausted), and B pays the remaining $50,000, for a total of $150,000. $187,500 would be B's share by limits.
source: ISO CG 00 01, Sec. IV Cond. 4.c Method Of Sharing; IRMI glossary: contribution by equal shares

q: A building worth $400,000 at the time of loss is insured for $240,000 under a commercial property policy with an 80% coinsurance clause and a $1,000 deductible. A $50,000 covered loss occurs. Using the ISO coinsurance formula, the insurer pays:
explain: Required insurance = $400,000 x 80% = $320,000. $240,000 / $320,000 = 0.75, so $50,000 x 0.75 = $37,500, less the $1,000 deductible = $36,500. The deductible is subtracted after the coinsurance calculation.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12, F.1 and D

q: A building worth $300,000 at the time of loss is insured for $200,000 with an 80% coinsurance clause and no deductible. It is totally destroyed by a covered fire. The insurer pays:
explain: Required = $240,000; $200,000 / $240,000 x $300,000 = $250,000. But the insurer pays that amount or the Limit of Insurance, whichever is less, so it pays $200,000.

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, a building has been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days when a covered windstorm damages it. The insurer will:
choices: Reduce the amount it would otherwise pay by 15%
Reduce the amount it would otherwise pay by 50%
explain: Under the 2012 edition, after 60 consecutive days of vacancy, vandalism, sprinkler leakage, building glass breakage, water damage, theft, and attempted theft are not covered. All other covered causes, such as windstorm, are reduced by 15%.

q: After a fire, the insured tells the insurer to take the damaged inventory and pay its full value. Under the Building and Personal Property Coverage Form:
choices: The insurer must accept the property and pay its full value
The insurer must accept the property if the insured files a sworn proof of loss within 60 days
Abandonment is allowed only for stock, not for buildings
There can be no abandonment of any property to the insurer
explain: The BPP Loss Conditions state: 'There can be no abandonment of any property to us.' The insurer may, at its option, take property at an agreed or appraised value, but the insured cannot force it to.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.1 and E.4.a

q: A liberalization clause provides that:
choices: The insured may broaden coverage mid-term without paying additional premium
The insurer may restrict coverage mid-term by giving the named insured 30 days' written notice
Coverage broadened by the insurer without additional premium automatically applies to existing policies
The insured may cancel at any time and receive a pro rata refund
explain: Liberalization extends broadened coverage to existing policies. The ISO commercial property version applies to revisions adopted within 45 days before or during the policy period; the ISO homeowners version uses 60 days.
source: ISO CP 00 90 07 88, E; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sections I and II Cond. A

q: After paying its insured for fire damage to a building caused by a negligent contractor, the insurer sues the contractor to recover what it paid. This right is called:
explain: Subrogation transfers to the insurer, after payment, the insured's right to recover from the party legally liable for the loss.
source: IRMI glossary: subrogation; ISO CP 00 90 07 88, I

q: An insurer denies an insured's fire claim because the insured committed arson. Under the standard mortgage clause of a Homeowners policy, the named mortgagee:
choices: Can still collect on a valid claim if it meets the clause's conditions
Loses its right to payment along with the insured
Must first obtain a judgment against the insured before the insurer will pay
Is entitled only to a return of the unearned premium
explain: The standard mortgage clause protects the mortgagee from the insured's acts if the mortgagee reports known changes in risk, pays premium due on demand, and submits a sworn statement of loss within 60 days after notice. A basic loss payable clause, such as the Homeowners loss payable condition, gives no such independent protection.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. L, S; IRMI glossary: loss payable clause

sub: Third-Party Provisions - No Benefit to the Bailee
q: A dry cleaner holding customers' clothing tries to have its liability for a fire at its plant paid by the customers' own property insurance. The policy provision that prevents this is:
explain: No person or organization, other than the insured, that has custody of covered property benefits from the insurance; the HO version specifically refers to those holding, storing, or moving property for a fee.
source: ISO CP 00 90 07 88, F; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. M

q: Under a Commercial General Liability (CGL) policy, the insurer's right and duty to defend ends when:
choices: Defense costs equal the each-occurrence limit
The insured is found more than 50% at fault
The applicable limit is used up in paying judgments or settlements
The policy period expires, even if the suit is still pending
explain: The CGL states the duty to defend ends when the applicable limit is used up paying judgments or settlements under Coverages A or B or medical expenses under C. Defense costs are paid as supplementary payments and do not erode limits.
source: ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. I Cov. A.1.a(2)

q: In an insurance transaction, a binder is:
choices: A permanent substitute for the policy
The insurer's approval of the producer's appointment
An endorsement that adds a mortgagee to the policy
explain: A binder is a legal agreement issued by an agent or insurer as temporary evidence of coverage. It should be in writing, have a definite time limit, and name the insurer.
source: IRMI glossary: binder

q: Which type of adjuster represents the insured rather than the insurance company?
explain: A public adjuster represents the insured in presenting a claim and is usually paid a percentage of the settlement. Staff adjusters are insurer employees; independent adjusters work for insurers on contract.
source: IRMI glossary: public adjuster; adjuster; independent adjuster

q: Under Michigan's timely-payment statute, if an insurer does not pay its own insured's claim within 60 days after receiving satisfactory proof of loss, the benefits bear simple interest at:
explain: MCL 500.2006(4): benefits not paid on a timely basis bear simple interest at 12% per annum from 60 days after the insurer receives satisfactory proof of loss. For the insured (or a person directly entitled under the policy) this interest is owed even if the claim was reasonably in dispute; the "not reasonably in dispute" and court-found bad-faith conditions apply only to third-party tort claimants.
source: MCL 500.2006(1), (3), (4); Griswold Props, LLC v Lexington Ins Co, 276 Mich App 551 (2007)

q: Under Michigan's timely-payment statute, unless a claim is settled sooner, an insurer must specify in writing what constitutes a satisfactory proof of loss within how many days after receiving the claim?
explain: The insurer must specify the required proof-of-loss materials in writing within 30 days after receiving a claim, unless the claim is settled within those 30 days. The 60-day period is the payment deadline after proof of loss.

q: Which of the following is NOT paid from the General Aggregate Limit of a Commercial General Liability (CGL) policy?
choices: Personal and advertising injury damages under Coverage B
Bodily injury from a customer's fall on the insured's premises
Bodily injury included in the products-completed operations hazard
explain: The General Aggregate covers Coverage C, Coverage B, and Coverage A except products-completed operations. Products-completed operations BI/PD has its own separate aggregate.
source: ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. III.2-3

q: Under a commercial policy with several named insureds, which insured is responsible for paying premium and receives cancellation notices and return premiums?
explain: Under the ISO Common Policy Conditions, the first named insured (listed first in the declarations) is responsible for paying all premiums, is the payee for return premiums, and is the one the insurer sends cancellation notice to. Other named insureds and additional insureds do not have these duties.
source: ISO IL 00 17 11 98, A and E; IRMI glossary: first named insured; NCCI WC 00 00 00 C, Part Six E

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, the only exception to workers' compensation being the employee's exclusive remedy against the employer is:
choices: A violation of an OSHA standard
An injury caused by a co-worker's negligence
explain: MCL 418.131(1): 'The only exception to this exclusive remedy is an intentional tort.' Negligence, including gross negligence, does not qualify.

q: The Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act deems an employer to have intended an employee's injury when the employer:
choices: Failed to provide safety training required by OSHA
Was grossly negligent in maintaining equipment that later injured the employee
Had actual knowledge that an injury was certain and willfully disregarded it
Knew an injury was possible and did not post a warning sign near the hazard
explain: An intentional tort requires a deliberate act with specific intent to injure; intent is deemed if the employer had actual knowledge that injury was certain to occur and willfully disregarded it. Whether an act was an intentional tort is a question of law for the court.

q: A private, non-agricultural Michigan employer has only 2 employees. It is subject to the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act if:
choices: Both employees have worked for it at least 20 hours per week for 30 days or longer
It has been in business for at least 1 year
At least 1 was regularly employed 35+ hours a week for 13+ of the past 52 weeks
explain: Private employers with fewer than 3 employees are covered if at least 1 has been regularly employed 35+ hours per week for 13+ weeks in the preceding 52 weeks. Employers that regularly employ 3 or more at one time are always covered.

q: A worker is disabled by a work injury for 3 weeks. Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, weekly compensation is:
choices: Computed from the date of injury
Paid beginning on the 8th day only
Paid beginning on the 15th day only
Not payable for the first week
explain: No compensation is paid for the first week unless incapacity lasts longer; compensation starts on the 8th day. If incapacity continues for 2 weeks or longer (or death results), compensation is computed from the date of injury.

q: Michigan's workers' compensation law sets weekly wage-loss benefits for total disability at what percentage of the employee's after-tax average weekly wage, subject to the state maximum?
explain: Total disability benefits are 80% of after-tax AWW, capped at the maximum weekly rate. The maximum itself is set at 90% of the state average weekly wage.

q: When a work injury causes death, the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act limits the employer's liability for funeral and burial expenses to:
choices: $5,000 or the actual cost, whichever is less
$6,000 or the actual cost, whichever is less
$10,000 or the actual cost, whichever is less
The actual cost, with no dollar limit
explain: MCL 418.345 caps the cost of the funeral and burial at $6,000 or the actual cost, whichever is less; the employer also pays the reasonable expense of the last sickness.

q: Under Michigan's specific loss schedule, the loss of a hand is compensated for:
explain: MCL 418.361(2): hand 215 weeks; arm 269; foot 162; leg 215; eye 162; thumb 65.

q: A worker who had previously lost an eye loses a leg in a work accident. Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, after the payments for the second loss end, the worker:
choices: Is conclusively presumed totally and permanently disabled and paid by the Second Injury Fund
Receives only the specific-loss weeks for the leg
Must prove total and permanent disability at a new hearing before any further benefits are paid
Is paid by the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility
explain: Loss of a second hand, arm, foot, leg, or eye after a prior such loss creates a conclusive presumption of total and permanent disability. The Second Injury Fund pays beginning at the end of payments for the second loss.

q: The Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility exists primarily to:
choices: Pay benefits to employees of insolvent workers' compensation insurers
Provide insurance to employers unable to obtain it through ordinary methods
Pay benefits to employees of uninsured employers
Set the rates that all Michigan workers' compensation insurers must use for each class
explain: Every insurer authorized to write workers' compensation in Michigan must participate in the facility, which provides coverage to those who cannot obtain it normally while encouraging maximum use of the private market.

q: A crew member injured aboard a Great Lakes freighter through the employer's negligence would ordinarily seek recovery under:
choices: The Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
explain: The Jones Act (now 46 USC 30104, formerly 46 USC 688) lets an injured seaman sue the employer for negligence with a jury trial. The LHWCA expressly excludes a master or member of the crew of any vessel.

q: The standard limits for Part Two – Employers Liability Insurance of the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy are:
choices: $100,000 each accident / $100,000 disease-policy limit / $500,000 disease-each employee
$100,000 each accident / $500,000 disease-policy limit / $100,000 disease-each employee
$500,000 each accident / $500,000 disease-policy limit / $500,000 disease-each employee
$1,000,000 each accident / $1,000,000 disease-policy limit / $1,000,000 disease-each employee
explain: The standard employers liability limits are $100,000 bodily injury by accident (each accident), $500,000 bodily injury by disease (policy limit) and $100,000 bodily injury by disease (each employee). The actual limits are shown in Item 3.B of the Information Page, and higher limits may be bought. (National standard. In Michigan, manual rules and experience mods come from CAOM, not NCCI.)
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C, Part Two G (limits in Item 3.B); national standard EL limits as reproduced in NCRB Basic Manual Rule 5; CAOM Michigan WC Placement Facility Basic Manual, Rule Eight (increased limits $500,000 / $1,000,000)

q: An employer's workers' compensation policy lists Michigan in Item 3.A and several other states, including Indiana, in Item 3.C. Midway through the policy term, the employer begins a job in Indiana and is not otherwise insured there. Coverage for the Indiana work:
choices: Applies as if Indiana were listed in Item 3.A, and the insurer must be told at once
Does not apply until Indiana is endorsed onto the policy at renewal
Applies only to employers liability, not to Indiana workers' compensation benefits
Applies only if the insurer is notified within 90 days after the Indiana work begins
explain: Part Three applies to states listed in Item 3.C. If work begins there after the effective date, the policy applies as though the state were in 3.A; the insured must notify the insurer at once. (The 30-day notice rule applies to work already underway on the effective date in a state not listed in 3.A.)
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Three A.2, A.4, B

q: An employer's payroll in one classification is $250,000, the rate is $4.00 per $100 of payroll, and its experience modification is 0.85. What is the premium after the experience modification is applied?
explain: Manual premium = ($250,000 / 100) x $4.00 = $10,000. Applying a 0.85 mod (a credit) gives $8,500. A mod above 1.00 would be a debit.
source: CAOM Michigan WC Placement Facility Basic Manual, Part One premium algorithm (Manual Premium = (Payroll/100) x Rate; x Experience Modification); IRMI glossary: manual premium; standard premium

q: An employer knowingly employs a 15-year-old in violation of child labor law. The minor is injured on the job, and Michigan law requires double compensation. Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, who ultimately bears the extra benefits above the regular statutory amount?
choices: The Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility
explain: Part One F makes the employer responsible for payments above regular benefits required because it knowingly employed someone in violation of law; if the insurer pays them, the employer must reimburse it. MCL 418.161(1)(l) provides double compensation for illegally employed minors under 18.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C, Part One F; MCL 418.161(1)(l)

q: The Voluntary Compensation and Employers Liability Coverage Endorsement is used to:
choices: Extend workers compensation coverage to the other states listed in Item 3.C
Cover employees subject to the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
Pay statutory-equivalent benefits to employees the employer need not cover by law
explain: The endorsement pays benefits equal to those of a designated WC law to scheduled employees not required to be covered (for example, farm or domestic workers). Before payment, the claimant must release the employer and insurer and transfer recovery rights to the insurer.
source: NCCI WC 00 03 11 A; IRMI glossary: voluntary compensation endorsement

q: The process of deciding whether to accept a risk and, if so, how much insurance to write on it and at what rate is called:
explain: Underwriting is the process of determining whether to accept a risk and, if so, what amount of insurance to write on it and at what rate. Subrogation is the insurer's right to recover a loss payment from a liable party, and reinsurance indemnifies an insurer for part or all of the liability it has assumed.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "underwriting"; "subrogation"; "reinsurance"

q: All of the following are underwriting decisions EXCEPT:
choices: How much to pay on a covered claim
How much insurance to write on an accepted risk
explain: Underwriting decides whether to accept a risk, how much insurance to write on it, and at what rate. Deciding the amount payable on a covered claim is part of claims handling, not underwriting.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "underwriting"

q: Oily rags stored next to a furnace in a commercial building are an example of a(n):
explain: A physical hazard is a material, structural, or operational feature that creates or increases the chance of loss; improperly stored oily rags make a fire more likely. Fire itself would be the peril (the cause of loss), while moral and morale hazards come from the insured's character or attitude.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "physical hazard"; "hazard"; "peril"; "moral hazard"; "morale hazard"

q: Which of the following is an example of a physical hazard?
choices: An applicant's prior conviction for insurance fraud
An insured's carelessness because insurance will pay
Inadequate lighting in a crime-prone area
explain: IRMI gives inadequate lighting in a crime-prone area as an example of a hazard, a condition that increases the probability of loss; it is a physical (material or operational) condition. A fraud conviction points to moral hazard, carelessness because insurance will pay is morale hazard, and a tornado is a peril.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "hazard"; "physical hazard"; "moral hazard"; "morale hazard"; "peril"

q: An applicant for fire insurance on a business that is losing money was previously convicted of insurance fraud. The underwriter is most concerned about:
explain: Moral hazard arises from the character or circumstances of the insured, such as dishonesty or a financial incentive to cause a loss; IRMI notes that insurance on an unprofitable business carries more moral hazard. Morale hazard is indifference to loss, and physical hazard is a tangible condition of the property.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "moral hazard"; "morale hazard"; "physical hazard"

q: Moral hazard differs from morale hazard because moral hazard arises from the insured's:
choices: Indifference to loss because insurance will pay
explain: Moral hazard reflects the character or circumstances of the insured, such as dishonesty. Morale hazard reflects attitude rather than integrity: indifference to loss because insurance will pay. The condition of a building is a physical hazard.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "moral hazard"; "morale hazard"; "physical hazard"

q: A jury awards an injured plaintiff $40,000 for medical bills and lost wages and $100,000 for pain and suffering. These awards are, respectively:
explain: Both awards are compensatory damages. Special damages are objectively measured, quantifiable losses such as medical expenses and wage loss; general damages are a subjective award for pain and suffering. Punitive damages go beyond compensation to punish the defendant.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "compensatory damages"; "special damages"; "general damages"; "punitive damages"

q: Which of the following is an example of general damages?
explain: General damages are a subjective award to compensate an injured person for pain and suffering. Lost wages, medical expenses, and nursing care are quantifiable, tangible losses, which are special damages.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "general damages"; "special damages"

q: A manufacturer is held liable for injuries caused by its dangerous product even though it used every possible care in making and selling the product. This is an example of:
explain: Strict liability is imposed without regard to fault or negligence; IRMI's example is the maker or distributor of a dangerous product, regardless of the care it exercised. Vicarious liability is a principal's liability for the acts of its agents, and comparative negligence reduces a plaintiff's recovery by the plaintiff's own fault.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "strict liability"; "vicarious liability"; "comparative negligence"

q: Strict liability is liability imposed:
choices: Without regard to fault or negligence
Only when the defendant breached a duty of reasonable care
Only when the defendant intended to cause harm
Only when the plaintiff was free of any fault
explain: Strict liability is liability imposed without regard to fault or negligence. Liability for breaching a duty of care owed to the plaintiff is negligence, which strict liability does not require.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "strict liability"; "negligence"

q: Ignoring the deductible, auto physical damage coverage written on a stated amount basis pays a covered loss based on the:
choices: Stated amount, even if it is more than the auto's actual cash value
Least of the actual cash value, the cost to repair or replace, or the stated amount
Greatest of the actual cash value, the cost to repair or replace, or the stated amount
Actual cash value, even if it is more than the stated amount
explain: Stated amount coverage limits payment to the least of the actual cash value, the cost to repair or replace with property of like kind and quality, or the stated amount shown in the schedule. The stated amount is a ceiling, not a guaranteed payment; unlike agreed value, the insured can receive less than the stated amount.
source: ISO CA 99 28 03 10 (Stated Amount Insurance, 2010 edition; Virginia SCC specimen copy via the Internet Archive, retrieved 2026-10-13), Schedule note and B. Limit Of Insurance 1.a-c; consistent carrier form: Essentia Insurance Co. AC 129 01 24 "Stated Value" endorsement, Part D Limit of Liability ("lesser of" the stated value, actual cash value, or repair/replace cost)

q: Under the 2010 ISO Stated Amount Insurance endorsement, a business's van has a $50,000 stated amount and a $1,000 deductible. It is totally destroyed in a covered collision. Its actual cash value is $42,000, and like kind and quality replacement costs $45,000. The insurer pays:
explain: The endorsement pays the least of the actual cash value ($42,000), the cost to replace with like kind and quality ($45,000), or the stated amount ($50,000), and the deductible reduces the actual cash value or replacement cost: $42,000 - $1,000 = $41,000. The $50,000 stated amount is only a ceiling; the schedule warns that it is not necessarily the amount the insured will receive.
source: ISO CA 99 28 03 10 (Stated Amount Insurance, 2010 edition; Virginia SCC specimen copy via the Internet Archive, retrieved 2026-10-13), Schedule note, B. Limit Of Insurance 1.a-c and 2., and C. Deductible 1.a-b

q: In ISO policy forms, words and phrases that appear in quotation marks:
choices: Are optional coverages that require an extra premium
Were added to the policy by an endorsement after issue
Are terms that state law requires in every policy
Have special meanings given in the definitions section
explain: ISO forms state that words and phrases in quotation marks have special meaning and refer the reader to the Definitions section (Section H in the Building and Personal Property Coverage Form; Section V in the CGL form).
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), preamble ("Other words and phrases that appear in quotation marks have special meaning. Refer to Section H. Definitions."); ISO CG 00 01 04 13 (Commercial General Liability Coverage Form, 2013 edition), preamble (Section V – Definitions); ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Definitions ("Other words and phrases are defined. They are in quotation marks when used.")

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, the words "you" and "your" refer to:
choices: The named insured and a spouse who lives in the same household
Only the named insured shown in the Declarations
Any licensed driver living in the named insured's household
Any person using a covered auto with permission
explain: The Definitions section defines "you" and "your" as the named insured shown in the Declarations and the spouse if a resident of the same household. A spouse who moves out remains "you" only until the earliest of 90 days, the effective date of another policy naming the spouse, or the end of the policy period; other resident relatives are "family members."
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Definitions A and F

sub: Policy Structure - Insuring Agreement or Clause
q: The part of an insurance policy that contains the insurer's promise to pay is the:
explain: The insuring agreement is the portion of the policy in which the insurer promises to make payment to or on behalf of the insured. It usually states a broad scope of coverage that exclusions and definitions then narrow.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "insuring agreement"

sub: Policy Structure - Insuring Agreement or Clause
q: A liability policy states: "We will pay those sums that the insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of 'bodily injury' or 'property damage' to which this insurance applies." This provision is part of the:
explain: This is the Coverage A Insuring Agreement of the CGL form: the insurer's promise to pay. Quoted terms such as "bodily injury" are explained in the Definitions section, and the Conditions set the parties' duties.
source: ISO CG 00 01 04 13 (Commercial General Liability Coverage Form, 2013 edition), Section I, Coverage A, 1. Insuring Agreement, a.; IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "insuring agreement"

q: Policy provisions that set out the rights and duties of the insured and the insurer, such as notice of loss, cancellation, and how other insurance is shared, are called:
explain: ISO forms place these rules in their Conditions sections. For example, the CGL Conditions include Duties In The Event Of Occurrence, Offense, Claim Or Suit and Other Insurance, and the Common Policy Conditions include Cancellation.
source: ISO CG 00 01 04 13 (Commercial General Liability Coverage Form, 2013 edition), Section IV – Commercial General Liability Conditions (2. Duties In The Event Of Occurrence, Offense, Claim Or Suit; 4. Other Insurance); ISO IL 00 17 11 98 (Common Policy Conditions, 1998 edition), A. Cancellation

q: In the 2011 ISO Homeowners policy (HO-3), the insured's duties to give prompt notice of a loss and to send a signed, sworn proof of loss appear in:
explain: Duties After Loss is a Section I condition in the HO-3. It requires prompt notice and a signed, sworn proof of loss within 60 days after the insurer's request, among other duties.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Conditions, C. Duties After Loss

q: A homeowners policy provision stating that the insurer does not insure for loss caused by flood or earthquake is a(n):
explain: An exclusion is a policy provision describing hazards, perils, circumstances, or property not covered. The HO-3 lists Earth Movement (including earthquake) and Water (including flood) among its Section I Exclusions.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "exclusion"; ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Exclusions, A.2 Earth Movement and A.3 Water

q: The purpose of the exclusions in an insurance policy is to:
choices: State the insurer's broad promise to pay for covered losses
Identify the named insured, policy period, location, and limits
Remove coverage for stated perils, property, or circumstances
Set out the insured's duties after a loss and other policy rules
explain: Exclusions describe the hazards, perils, circumstances, or property the policy does not cover, narrowing the broad insuring agreement. The promise to pay is the insuring agreement, the named insured and limits are in the Declarations, and duties after loss are conditions.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "exclusion"; "insuring agreement"; "declarations"

q: A form that changes a policy by broadening or restricting coverage, or by adding an insured or a location, is a(n):
explain: An endorsement is a form that changes or adds to the provisions of the other forms making up the policy, for example by broadening or restricting coverage, adding insureds, or adding locations. A binder is only temporary evidence of insurance.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "endorsement"; "binder"

q: Under the 1998 ISO Common Policy Conditions, a commercial policy's terms can be amended or waived only by:
choices: Written notice from the first Named Insured to the insurer
A binder issued by the producer
An oral agreement between the producer and the first Named Insured
An endorsement issued by the insurer and made part of the policy
explain: The Changes condition says the policy's terms can be amended or waived only by endorsement issued by the insurer and made part of the policy. The first Named Insured may make changes only with the insurer's consent. The 2018 Personal Auto Policy has a similar Changes provision.
source: ISO IL 00 17 11 98 (Common Policy Conditions, 1998 edition), B. Changes; ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part F – General Provisions, Changes A

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, the policy applies only to accidents and losses that occur:
choices: During the policy period, anywhere in the world
During the policy period and within the policy territory
Within the policy territory, if reported during the policy period
During the policy period or within 30 days after it ends
explain: The Policy Period and Territory provision states that the policy applies only to accidents and losses that occur during the policy period shown in the Declarations and within the policy territory.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part F – General Provisions, Policy Period and Territory A

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, Section I property coverage applies only to loss that:
choices: Is first reported to the insurer during the policy period
Is discovered during the policy period, whenever it occurred
Occurs during the policy period or within 30 days after it ends
explain: The Section I Policy Period condition states that the policy applies only to loss which occurs during the policy period. Section II similarly applies only to bodily injury or property damage that occurs during the policy period.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Conditions, Q. Policy Period; Section II – Conditions, I. Policy Period

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, the policy territory includes all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Territories and possessions of the United States
explain: The policy territory is the United States of America, its territories or possessions, Puerto Rico, and Canada. It also covers a covered auto while being transported between their ports. Mexico is not included.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part F – General Provisions, Policy Period and Territory B

q: Under the 1988 ISO Commercial Property Conditions, the coverage territory is the United States (including its territories and possessions) plus:
explain: The Commercial Property Conditions cover loss commencing during the policy period and within the coverage territory: the United States of America (including its territories and possessions), Puerto Rico, and Canada.
source: ISO CP 00 90 07 88 (Commercial Property Conditions, 1988 edition), H. Policy Period, Coverage Territory

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, a building has a $60,000 Limit of Insurance and a $250 deductible. A covered fire causes $70,000 of damage, and no coinsurance penalty applies. The insurer pays:
explain: The insurer subtracts the deductible from the loss and pays the result or the Limit of Insurance, whichever is less: $70,000 - $250 = $69,750, capped at the $60,000 limit. The deductible is not subtracted from the limit, as the form's Example 2 shows.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), D. Deductible and Example 2; IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "deductible"

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, if two or more deductibles under the policy apply to the same loss:
choices: Each deductible applies to its own part of the loss
explain: The Section I Deductible condition provides that if two or more deductibles under the policy apply to the loss, only the highest deductible amount will apply.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Conditions, B. Deductible, 2.

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, one fire damages two buildings that have separate Limits of Insurance. The deductible is applied:
choices: Once for each location shown in the Declarations
Once for each Covered Cause of Loss involved
explain: When an occurrence damages more than one item with separate Limits of Insurance, the losses are not combined in applying the deductible, but the deductible is applied only once per occurrence.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), D. Deductible and Example 1

q: Two policies cover the same building, but one runs from January 1 to January 1 and the other from April 1 to April 1. This condition is called:
explain: Nonconcurrency is the condition created when two or more policies covering the same loss exposure do not have identical inception and expiration dates. Contribution by equal shares and pro rata (contribution by limits) are methods of sharing a loss among insurers.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "nonconcurrency"; "contribution by equal shares"; "contribution by limits"

q: A 2013 ISO CGL policy has a $1,000,000 Each Occurrence Limit and an unused $2,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. One explosion at the insured's store injures three customers, whose covered bodily injury damages total $1,500,000. The most the insurer will pay for these damages is:
explain: The Each Occurrence Limit is the most the insurer will pay for Coverage A damages and Coverage C medical expenses from all bodily injury and property damage arising out of any one occurrence, regardless of the number of people making claims. The aggregate limit does not raise the per-occurrence cap.
source: ISO CG 00 01 04 13 (Commercial General Liability Coverage Form, 2013 edition), Section III – Limits of Insurance, 1., 2. and 5.; IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "per occurrence limit"

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, Sam's bodily injury limits are $100,000 each person and $300,000 each accident. He is legally liable for an accident that injures four people, each with $100,000 of damages. The insurer pays a total of:
explain: Each person can receive up to $100,000, which would total $400,000, but the each-accident limit is the most the insurer will pay for all bodily injury from one auto accident, regardless of the number of claims. The insurer pays $300,000.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part A – Liability Coverage, Limit of Liability A

q: A policy's bodily injury limits are $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident. The insured is legally liable for an accident injuring two people, with damages of $25,000 and $75,000. The most the insurer pays the second person is:
explain: The per-person limit is the most the insurer will pay for any one person's injuries. The first claimant receives $25,000 and the second is capped at the $50,000 per-person limit, for a total of $75,000, within the per-accident limit.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "per person limit" (same example)

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, Jo has bodily injury liability limits of $100,000 each person and $300,000 each accident. Jo is legally liable for an accident that injures three people, with damages of $150,000, $50,000 and $40,000. The insurer pays a total of:
explain: Each injured person is capped at the $100,000 each-person limit, so the payments are $100,000 + $50,000 + $40,000 = $190,000. That total is within the $300,000 each-accident limit.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part A – Liability Coverage, Limit of Liability A

q: An auto liability policy has split limits of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000. The $25,000 figure is the most the insurer will pay for:
choices: Bodily injury to any one person
All bodily injury in one accident
All property damage in one accident
explain: With split limits, three separate amounts apply to each accident: a per-person bodily injury limit, a per-accident limit for all bodily injury, and a per-accident limit for property damage. The third figure is the property damage limit.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "split limits"; ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part A – Liability Coverage, Limit of Liability A

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, Lee has split liability limits of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000. Lee is legally liable for an accident that injures two people, with damages of $70,000 and $40,000, and causes $30,000 of property damage. The insurer pays a total of:
explain: Bodily injury: $50,000 (per-person cap) + $40,000 = $90,000, within the $100,000 per-accident limit. Property damage is capped at $25,000. Total: $90,000 + $25,000 = $115,000.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "split limits"; "per person limit"; ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part A – Liability Coverage, Limit of Liability A

q: A single dollar limit that applies to any combination of bodily injury and property damage liability claims from one accident is a(n):
explain: A combined single limit is one dollar limit for any combination of bodily injury and property damage liability claims. Split limits instead apply three separate amounts per accident. The Business Auto Coverage Form's Covered Autos Liability limit works this way.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "combined single limits"; ISO CA 00 01 10 13 (Business Auto Coverage Form, 2013 edition), Section II – Covered Autos Liability Coverage, C. Limit Of Insurance

q: An auto liability policy has a $300,000 combined single limit. The insured is legally liable for an accident that injures two people, with damages of $150,000 and $120,000, and causes $60,000 of property damage. The insurer pays a total of:
explain: A combined single limit applies to bodily injury and property damage together, with no separate per-person or property damage limit. Total damages are $330,000, so the insurer pays the $300,000 limit.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "combined single limits"; ISO CA 00 01 10 13 (Business Auto Coverage Form, 2013 edition), Section II, C. Limit Of Insurance (single limit for the total of all damages from any one accident)

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, the most the insurer will pay for loss or damage in any one occurrence is:
choices: The actual cash value of the damaged property, even if more than the limit
The replacement cost of the damaged property, even if more than the limit
The applicable Limit of Insurance shown in the Declarations
The amount the insured originally paid for the property
explain: The Limits of Insurance section states that the most the insurer will pay for loss or damage in any one occurrence is the applicable Limit of Insurance shown in the Declarations.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), C. Limits Of Insurance

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, amounts paid under all of the following Additional Coverages are separate from the Limit of Insurance EXCEPT:
explain: Fire Department Service Charge, Pollutant Clean-up and Removal, Increased Cost of Construction, and Electronic Data amounts are separate from the Limit of Insurance. Payments under Preservation of Property do not increase the applicable Limit of Insurance.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), C. Limits Of Insurance

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, a named insured dies during the policy period. Coverage continues for the surviving spouse who lived in the same household:
choices: Until the end of the policy period
Until the insurer approves an assignment of the policy
explain: The insured's rights and duties may not be assigned without the insurer's written consent. However, if a named insured dies, coverage is provided for the surviving spouse (if a resident of the same household at the time of death) as if a named insured, and for the legal representative with respect to the covered auto, but only until the end of the policy period.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part F – General Provisions, Transfer Of Your Interest In This Policy A. and B.; IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "assignment"

q: Under the 1998 ISO Common Policy Conditions, the named insured's rights and duties under a commercial policy may be transferred without the insurer's written consent:
choices: When the insured property is sold
Only if an individual named insured dies
When the first Named Insured gives 10 days' notice
When the transfer is to an affiliated business
explain: Rights and duties may not be transferred without the insurer's written consent except in the case of the death of an individual named insured. They then pass to the legal representative, acting within the scope of that role.
source: ISO IL 00 17 11 98 (Common Policy Conditions, 1998 edition), F. Transfer Of Your Rights And Duties Under This Policy

q: In property insurance, the term salvage refers to:
choices: Damaged property that remains after a loss by an insured peril
The insurer's right to recover its payment from a negligent third party
Payment of a loss to a lender named in the policy
The insured's duty to give prompt notice of a loss
explain: Salvage is property after it has been partially damaged by an insured peril such as fire; as a verb, it means saving endangered property and protecting damaged property from further loss. Recovering from a negligent third party is subrogation, and paying a lender is done under a loss payable clause.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "salvage"; "subrogation"; "loss payable clause"

q: An auto insurer pays a total loss claim, takes ownership of the wrecked car, and sells it to an automotive recycler. The wrecked car is:
explain: Salvage is damaged property remaining after a loss; the insurer may take it when it pays the claim (the Personal Auto Policy lets the insurer keep all or part of the property at an agreed or appraised value). Michigan's Vehicle Code sets salvage and scrap title rules for late model vehicles an insurer acquires by paying a claim.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "salvage"; ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part D, Payment of Loss; MCL 257.217c(2)

q: Under the 2012 ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, who chooses whether a covered loss is settled by paying its value, paying to repair or replace, taking the property at an agreed or appraised value, or rebuilding?
explain: The Loss Payment condition gives these four settlement options "at our option," meaning the insurer's option. The insurer must give notice of its intentions within 30 days after receiving the sworn proof of loss.
source: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (Building and Personal Property Coverage Form, 2012 edition), E.4 Loss Payment, a. and c.

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, the insurer may repair or replace damaged property with property of like kind and quality if it gives written notice within how many days after receiving the signed, sworn proof of loss?
explain: The Our Option condition lets the insurer repair or replace any part of the damaged property with like kind and quality if it gives written notice within 30 days after receiving the signed, sworn proof of loss. In the unendorsed form, 60 days is the Loss Payment timing, a different condition.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Conditions, I. Our Option and J. Loss Payment

q: Under the 2018 ISO Personal Auto Policy, the insurer may settle a physical damage loss in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
choices: Paying the original purchase price regardless of actual cash value
Paying for the loss in money, including applicable sales tax
Repairing or replacing the damaged or stolen property
Keeping all or part of the property at an agreed or appraised value
explain: Under Payment of Loss, the insurer may pay in money or repair or replace the damaged or stolen property, and it may keep all or part of the property at an agreed or appraised value. Its limit is the lesser of actual cash value or the cost to repair or replace with like kind and quality, not the original purchase price.
source: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (Personal Auto Policy, 2018 edition), Part D – Coverage for Damage to Your Auto, Limit of Liability A and Payment of Loss

q: A clause providing for payment of a covered loss to a party other than the named insured that has an insurable interest, such as an auto lender, is a:
explain: A loss payable clause authorizes payment of a loss to a person or entity other than the named insured that has an insurable interest in the covered property, such as a lender financing a vehicle, "as its interest may appear."
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "loss payable clause"

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, the Declarations show a loss payee for a listed item of personal property. If the insurer decides to cancel the policy, it must:
choices: Obtain the loss payee's written consent
Pay any return premium to the loss payee
Notify the loss payee in writing
explain: Under the Loss Payable Clause, the loss payee is treated as an "insured" for the listed property, and if the insurer decides to cancel or not renew the policy, the loss payee will be notified in writing.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (Homeowners 3 – Special Form, 2011 edition), Section I – Conditions, S. Loss Payable Clause

q: A contract provision in which one party agrees to take on certain legal liabilities of the other party is a(n):
explain: A hold harmless (indemnity) agreement requires one contracting party to respond to certain legal liabilities of the other, such as a contractor indemnifying a project owner for injuries to the public during the work.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "hold harmless agreement"

q: A contractor agrees to hold the owner harmless for claims arising from the contractor's sole negligence or the joint negligence of the contractor and owner, but not the owner's sole negligence. This is a(n):
explain: An intermediate form covers the other party for the indemnitor's sole negligence or the negligence of both parties. A limited form covers only the indemnitor's sole negligence, and a broad form also covers the other party's sole negligence.
source: IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "hold harmless agreement"

q: Under Michigan law, a provision in a building construction contract that requires the contractor to indemnify the owner for bodily injury caused by the owner's sole negligence is:
choices: Enforceable if it is in writing and signed
Enforceable only up to the contract price
Void only if the owner is a public entity
explain: Michigan law makes a provision in a construction contract that indemnifies the promisee against liability for bodily injury or property damage caused by the promisee's sole negligence against public policy, void, and unenforceable. This rule applies to all such contracts, not only public ones; a separate subsection adds limits on what a public entity may require. Indemnifying the other party's sole negligence is the broad form of hold harmless agreement.
source: MCL 691.991(1) and (2) (1966 PA 165, as amended by 2012 PA 468, eff. Mar. 1, 2013); IRMI Glossary (irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions, retrieved 2026-10-13): "hold harmless agreement"

q: The uncertainty about whether a loss will occur is called:
explain: Risk is the uncertainty arising from the possible occurrence of a loss. A hazard is a condition that increases the chance of loss, a peril is the cause of loss, and an exposure is the state of being subject to loss.
source: IRMI glossary: risk; hazard; peril; exposure. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): risk

q: A pure risk is one that involves:
choices: The chance of loss or gain
Only the chance of loss or no loss
A condition that increases the chance of loss
explain: Pure risk presents a chance of loss or no loss, with no chance of gain, and is generally insurable. A chance of loss or gain is speculative risk, a condition that increases the chance of loss is a hazard, and the cause of a loss is a peril.
source: IRMI glossary: pure risk; speculative risk; hazard; peril. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): pure risk; speculative risk

q: Which of the following is an example of a speculative risk?
choices: A house being damaged by fire
Investing money in a new business
An employee being injured at work
explain: Speculative risk can produce either a profit or a loss, as in a business venture or gambling, and is generally not insurable. The other choices are pure risks, which offer only the chance of loss or no loss.
source: IRMI glossary: speculative risk; pure risk. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): speculative risk ("often referred to as a business risk")

q: Being subject to the possibility of loss from some hazard or contingency is called:
explain: Exposure is the state of being subject to loss because of some hazard or contingency; the word also means the rating unit or premium base of a risk. A hazard increases the chance of loss, and a peril is the cause of loss.
source: IRMI glossary: exposure; hazard; peril; adverse selection

q: A windstorm tears the roof off a house. In insurance terms, the windstorm is the:
explain: A peril is a cause of loss, such as fire, windstorm or collision. The damage to the roof is the loss, and a hazard is a condition that increases the chance of loss.
source: IRMI glossary: peril; hazard. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): peril ("The cause of a loss"); loss

q: A fire damages a store's inventory. In insurance terms, the reduction in the inventory's value is the:
explain: A loss is a reduction in value, and it is the basis of a claim under the policy. The fire that caused it is the peril.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): loss ("A reduction in value"); peril. IRMI glossary: loss; peril

q: A business chooses a $10,000 deductible on its property policy to lower its premium. For the first $10,000 of each covered loss, the business is using which method of handling risk?
explain: Risk retention is the planned acceptance of losses through deductibles, deliberate noninsurance and loss-sensitive plans. The part of each loss above the deductible is transferred to the insurer.
source: IRMI glossary: risk retention. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): active retention

q: A large company sets aside its own funds to pay its property losses as they occur instead of buying insurance. This self-insurance plan is a form of:
explain: Self-insurance is a formal decision to retain risk rather than insure it: the firm pays losses from a fund of its own money. No risk is shifted to another party.
source: IRMI glossary: self-insurance. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): self-insurance; retention

q: A method of handling risk in which a potential loss exposure is distributed among a number of persons is called:
explain: Sharing distributes a potential loss among a group; in risk sharing, each member's premiums and losses are allocated within the group by a predetermined formula. Retention is one party accepting its own losses.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): sharing; retention. IRMI glossary: risk sharing; risk retention

q: A business owner buys a commercial property policy so that an insurer, not the business, pays for covered losses. This method of handling risk is:
explain: Transfer shifts the uncertainty of loss to another party; buying insurance shifts it to the insurer. The business still owns the property, so the risk has not been avoided.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): transfer. IRMI glossary: noninsurance risk transfer (transfer to a party other than an insurer)

q: A construction contract requires the contractor to indemnify the project owner for the owner's liability to the public arising from the contractor's work. For the owner, this is an example of:
explain: A hold harmless (indemnity) agreement is a noninsurance transfer: by contract, it shifts the owner's liability to another party, here the contractor. No insurance policy is involved.
source: IRMI glossary: hold harmless agreement; noninsurance risk transfer. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): non-insurance contractual transfer

q: An insurer that has a capital fund paid in by stockholders, in addition to its surplus and reserves, is a:
explain: A stock company has a capital fund paid in by stockholders in addition to surplus and reserves. Mutual companies have no stockholders, a reciprocal is an unincorporated group of subscribers managed by an attorney-in-fact, and Lloyd's of London is a marketplace of independent underwriters rather than an insurance company.
source: IRMI glossary: stock company; mutual company; reciprocal; Lloyd's of London

q: The owners of a stock insurance company are:
choices: Stockholders who need not be insureds
explain: A stock insurer is owned by stockholders who are not necessarily insureds. A mutual is owned by its policyholders, and a reciprocal's subscribers act through an attorney-in-fact.
source: IRMI glossary: mutual company; stock company; reciprocal. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): stock company

q: A mutual insurance company is owned by its:
explain: A mutual company is owned by its insureds: every owner is an insured and every insured is an owner. A stock company is owned by stockholders.
source: IRMI glossary: mutual company. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): mutual company

sub: Authority and Powers of Producers > Express
q: Authority that an insurer specifically gives a producer, orally or in writing, is:
explain: Express authority is authority expressly given by the insurer, either orally or in writing, such as the powers spelled out in the agency contract. Apparent authority, which is tied to estoppel, rests on what a third party reasonably believes from the insurer's conduct.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): express authority; apparent authority. IRMI glossary: express authority; apparent agency. Cornell LII Wex: express authority

sub: Authority and Powers of Producers > Implied
q: Authority that the insurer has not specifically stated, but that is consistent with the producer fully exercising the authority the insurer did grant, is:
explain: Implied authority covers acts that are not spelled out but are consistent with, and reasonably necessary to, carrying out the express authority. Express authority is stated orally or in writing, and apparent authority rests on what a third party reasonably believes from the insurer's conduct.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): implied authority; express authority; apparent authority. IRMI glossary: implied authority. Cornell LII Wex: implied authority

sub: Authority and Powers of Producers > Implied
q: A producer's agency agreement authorizes her to collect premiums but says nothing about receipts. Her authority to give customers receipts, a step reasonably necessary to complete the collections, is:
explain: When a principal expressly authorizes a task, the agent also has implied authority to take the steps reasonably necessary to complete it. The power is not express because the agreement does not state it, and it is not apparent authority because it comes from the grant itself, not from a third party's belief.
source: Cornell LII Wex: implied authority; apparent authority. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): implied authority

sub: Elements of a Legal Contract > Offer and Acceptance
q: Under Michigan case law, an application for insurance is:
choices: An acceptance of the terms the insurer has offered to the applicant
An offer that the insurer must accept before a contract exists
A binding contract as soon as the applicant signs and dates it
A binder that provides temporary coverage until a policy is issued
explain: The Michigan Supreme Court describes an application for insurance as a mere offer that must be accepted before a contract of insurance comes into existence. A binder is a separate, temporary evidence of insurance issued by an agent or insurer.
source: Gorham v Peerless Life Ins Co, 368 Mich 335 (1962); IRMI glossary: binder

sub: Elements of a Legal Contract > Offer and Acceptance
q: When an applicant submits an application for insurance, the insurer generally accepts the applicant's offer by:
choices: Issuing a policy or a binder
Ordering an inspection of the property
Assigning the application to an underwriter
explain: An application is only an offer, and under Michigan case law the insurer's silence or inaction generally is not acceptance. The insurer accepts by issuing the policy or a binder; Michigan law treats a binder as a contract for temporary insurance that includes the terms and conditions of the policy applied for.
source: Gorham v Peerless Life Ins Co, 368 Mich 335 (1962); MCL 500.2250; IRMI glossary: binder; National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): application

sub: Elements of a Legal Contract > Competent Parties
q: The element of a legal contract that requires each party to be of legal age and to have the mental capacity to understand the agreement is:
explain: A competent party has the legal capacity to contract: legal age, the mental capacity to understand the contract, and freedom from duress. The Michigan Supreme Court lists parties competent to contract as the first element of a valid contract.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): competent party; contract law. AFT Michigan v Michigan, 497 Mich 197 (2015)

sub: Elements of a Legal Contract > Competent Parties
q: Under Michigan law, a person becomes an adult of legal age, with full legal capacity to enter into contracts, at age:
explain: Michigan's Age of Majority Act makes a person who is at least 18 an adult of legal age for all purposes, with the same legal capacity that was formerly acquired at 21. A separate Insurance Code rule lets a person aged 16 to 18 make a valid life or disability insurance contract, but it does not make that person an adult of legal age.
source: MCL 722.52(1) (Age of Majority Act of 1971); MCL 500.2205

sub: Elements of a Legal Contract > Legal Purpose
q: A policy written to insure a shipment of illegal drugs against theft would be unenforceable because the contract lacks:
explain: A valid contract must have a legal purpose (a proper subject matter). Michigan courts treat contracts founded on acts prohibited by statute, or that violate public policy, as void or unenforceable.
source: AFT Michigan v Michigan, 497 Mich 197 (2015); Maids Int'l, Inc v Saunders, Inc, 224 Mich App 508 (1997) (citing Mahoney v Lincoln Brick Co, 304 Mich 694 (1943)); Terrien v Zwit, 467 Mich 56 (2002); National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): contract law

q: Kate sells her home during the policy period and wants the buyer to take over her Homeowners policy (HO-3). The assignment of the policy is valid only if:
choices: The insurer gives its written consent
The buyer pays the remaining premium
Kate gives the insurer written notice of the sale
