explain: The Homeowners policy states that assignment of the policy will not be valid unless the insurer gives its written consent; notice from the insured is not consent. Because insurance is a personal contract with the insured, the policy does not pass to the buyer with the house.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sections I and II - Conditions, E. Assignment (same wording in HO 00 02 10 00, Sections I and II - Conditions, E., and DP 00 01 07 88, Condition 21); National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): assignment

q: An insurance policy is called a unilateral contract because:
choices: Only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise
The insurer alone drafts the policy wording
The values exchanged by the parties are unequal
The policy cannot be assigned without the insurer's consent
explain: In a unilateral contract only one party makes an enforceable promise: the insurer promises to pay covered claims, while the insured only has to meet conditions such as paying premiums and reporting losses. One-sided drafting describes a contract of adhesion, and an unequal exchange describes an aleatory contract.
source: IRMI glossary: unilateral contract; contract of adhesion; aleatory contract

q: Under the Homeowners policy (HO-3), the insurer has no duty to provide coverage if the insured's failure to give prompt notice of a property loss prejudices the insurer. This shows that an insurance policy is a(n):
explain: In a conditional contract, the insurer's promise depends on certain things occurring or being done, such as the insured performing the duties after loss. The Homeowners form says the insurer has no duty to provide coverage if failure to perform those duties is prejudicial to it.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): conditional contract. ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Section I - Conditions, C. Duties After Loss (same wording in HO 00 02 10 00, Section I - Conditions, B.)

q: The principle that an insurance payment should restore the insured to the financial position the insured had before the loss is:
explain: Indemnity means restoring an injured party to the financial position enjoyed before a loss, so the insured should not profit from the loss. Policy provisions that pay no insured more than its interest in the property apply this principle.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): indemnity. ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Section I - Conditions, A. Insurable Interest And Limit Of Liability; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.4.d

q: A homeowner has a $50,000 covered fire loss. Two property policies cover the home, each with a $100,000 limit. Ignoring deductibles, the principle of indemnity limits the homeowner's total recovery from both policies to:
explain: Indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss position without profit, so total recovery cannot exceed the $50,000 loss. Other-insurance clauses enforce this; under the 2011 Homeowners form, for example, each policy would pay only its proportional share, here $25,000.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): indemnity. IRMI glossary: other insurance clause. ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Section I - Conditions, G. Other Insurance And Service Agreement

q: Insurance contracts presume that both the applicant and the insurer will fully disclose all pertinent facts. This principle is called:
explain: Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) means the parties rely heavily on each other's honesty and presume full disclosure of all pertinent facts. That is why concealment of pertinent information can void a policy.
source: IRMI glossary: uberrimae fidei; concealment. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): utmost good faith

q: A statement in an application that the applicant believes to be true to the best of the applicant's knowledge is a(n):
explain: A representation is a statement in an application that the applicant represents as correct to the best of their knowledge, while a warranty guarantees that a fact is true. If the insurer relied on a representation that was false when made, it may have grounds to void the contract.
source: IRMI glossary: representation; warranty

q: Under Michigan law, a misrepresentation in an application for property insurance does not void the policy or defeat recovery unless the misrepresentation was:
choices: Related to the cause of the loss
explain: Michigan law says no misrepresentation avoids an insurance contract or defeats recovery unless it was material, meaning the insurer would have refused to make the contract had it known the facts. The statute does not require that the misstatement relate to the cause of the loss or be discovered before a loss.

q: A statement of fact about the risk that the insured guarantees to be true, and that will void the policy if it is untrue, is a:
explain: A warranty is a statement of fact given by the insured about the risk that will void the policy if untrue; it guarantees that something is true. A representation is a statement only believed true to the best of the applicant's knowledge.
source: IRMI glossary: warranty; representation. National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): warranty

q: What distinguishes fraud from an innocent misstatement of fact in an insurance application?
choices: Whether a producer completed the application
explain: Fraud is an intentional manipulation of the truth that another party relies on to its detriment, while a misrepresentation is simply a misstatement of facts. Proof of fraud in procuring insurance may lead the insurer to deny coverage and void the policy.
source: National Alliance Research Academy insurance glossary (riskeducation.org): fraud; misrepresentations. IRMI glossary: fraud

q: Under the 1988 ISO Commercial Property Conditions, fraud by the named insured relating to the Coverage Part voids the coverage if it occurs:
choices: Before the policy is issued, but not after
After a loss occurs, but not before
During the policy period, but not after it ends
explain: The Concealment, Misrepresentation Or Fraud condition voids the Coverage Part in any case of fraud by the named insured relating to it at any time. The Coverage Part is also void if any insured intentionally conceals or misrepresents a material fact at any time.
source: ISO CP 00 90 07 88, A. Concealment, Misrepresentation Or Fraud

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, an employee is entitled to compensation for a personal injury that:
choices: Arises out of and in the course of employment
Is reported to the employer within 30 days after it occurs
Is not caused by the employee's own carelessness
explain: Section 301(1) pays compensation for a personal injury "arising out of and in the course of employment". The employee does not have to prove the employer was negligent, and the employee's own ordinary carelessness does not bar benefits; only an injury caused by the employee's intentional and willful misconduct is not compensable (Section 305). The employee's notice of injury is due within 90 days, and late notice is excused unless the employer proves it was prejudiced.

q: An employee breaks an ankle during a company softball game whose major purpose is social and recreational. Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, the injury is:
choices: Covered for both medical and wage-loss benefits
Covered only if the game was on the employer's premises
explain: Section 301(3) states that an injury incurred in the pursuit of an activity whose major purpose is social or recreational is not covered, notwithstanding the on-premises presumption for employees going to or from work. A lawsuit brought for such an injury is not subject to the Act's exclusive-remedy section (Section 131).

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, an employee going to or from work who is on the work premises within a reasonable time before or after working hours is:
choices: Presumed to be in the course of employment
Outside the course of employment until the shift begins
Covered only if the employer's negligence caused the injury
explain: Section 301(3) presumes that an employee going to or from work, while on the premises where the work is to be performed and within a reasonable time before and after working hours, is in the course of employment. The presumption does not reach an injury from an activity whose major purpose is social or recreational.

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, a disease is compensable as a personal injury when it:
choices: Is an ordinary disease of life that the public is also exposed to outside of work
Was first diagnosed while the employee was on the employer's payroll
Is due to conditions characteristic of and peculiar to the employer's business
Is confirmed by a physician the employer selects
explain: Section 401(2)(b) defines personal injury to include a disease or disability due to causes and conditions characteristic of and peculiar to the employer's business that arises out of and in the course of the employment. An ordinary disease of life to which the public is generally exposed outside the employment is not compensable.

q: An employee contracted an occupational disease in the same type of work performed for three successive employers. Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, compensation for the disease is recoverable from:
choices: The first employer in that employment
Each employer in proportion to the time worked for it
The last employer in that employment
explain: Section 435 makes the total compensation recoverable from the employer who last employed the employee in the employment to which the disease was due and in which it was contracted. If liability is disputed, the employee claims against, and applies for a hearing against, the last employer only.

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, a claim for an occupational disease must be made within 2 years after:
choices: The employee's first exposure to the workplace conditions that caused the disease
The employee knew or reasonably should have known the disease was work related
The disease was first diagnosed, even if not yet known to be work related
The employer first received notice of the disease
explain: Section 441 requires an occupational disease claim within 2 years after the date the employee (or a deceased employee's dependents) had knowledge or a reasonable belief, or through ordinary diligence could have discovered, that the disease or death was work related. The period runs from that discovery of the work connection, not from the date of first exposure, a diagnosis that does not reveal the work connection, or the employer's notice.

q: The Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA) applies to employees of:
explain: FELA makes every common carrier by railroad engaged in interstate or foreign commerce liable in damages to its employees injured through its negligence; it does not reach other kinds of carriers or employers. Shipyard and marine terminal workers fall under the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act.
source: 45 U.S.C. 51 (FELA sec. 1); 33 U.S.C. 902(3), 903(a) (U.S. Code text via LII)

q: An interstate railroad worker is injured on the job and sues under the Federal Employers' Liability Act. To recover, the worker must generally prove that:
choices: The injury arose out of employment, with no showing of fault needed
The railroad's negligence caused the injury in whole or in part
The railroad intended to cause the injury
explain: FELA is a negligence law: the railroad is liable in damages for injury resulting in whole or in part from the negligence of its officers, agents or employees, or from defects in its equipment due to its negligence. The worker's own contributory negligence does not bar recovery but reduces damages in proportion, and there is no reduction if the railroad's violation of a safety statute contributed to the injury.
source: 45 U.S.C. 51, 53 (U.S. Code text via LII)

q: A private shipyard's employee is injured while repairing a cargo ship on a dry dock adjoining navigable waters of the United States. Which federal law provides compensation for this injury?
choices: The Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
The Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act
explain: The Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act covers persons in maritime employment, including ship repairmen, for injuries on navigable waters of the United States or an adjoining pier, wharf, dry dock, terminal or similar area, and pays compensation irrespective of fault. The Jones Act applies to seamen (vessel crew members, whom the Longshore Act excludes), and FELA applies to railroad workers.

q: A Michigan employer's Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy lists only Michigan in Item 3.A. Some of its employees are subject to the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act. Coverage for its obligations under that act:
choices: Is included in Part Three – Other States Insurance
Requires listing the act in Item 3.A
explain: The policy defines workers compensation law as the law of each state named in Item 3.A and excludes any federal workers compensation law, and Part Two excludes bodily injury in work subject to the Longshore Act. Michigan's Placement Facility manual states that Longshore Act coverage may be provided only by adding the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act Coverage Endorsement, and that the act is not to be entered in Item 3.A.
source: NCCI Workers Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), General Section C and Part Two C.8; Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (2026 edition, Ed. 09/26), Rule Two A and Rule Eleven B (endorsement WC 00 01 06 A)

q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the term "workers compensation law" includes:
choices: Federal workers compensation and occupational disease laws
The provisions of any law that provide nonoccupational disability benefits
The occupational disease law of each Item 3.A state
explain: The General Section defines workers compensation law as the workers compensation law and occupational disease law of each state or territory named in Item 3.A, including amendments in effect during the policy period. It does not include any federal workers compensation or occupational disease law, or laws that provide nonoccupational disability benefits.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), General Section C

q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the terms of the policy may be changed or waived only by:
choices: An endorsement issued by the insurer
An oral agreement between the producer and the employer
A written notice from the employer to the insurer
A letter from the producer to the employer
explain: General Section A states that the only agreements relating to the insurance are stated in the policy, and its terms may not be changed or waived except by endorsement issued by the insurer to be part of the policy. The policy includes the Information Page and all endorsements and schedules listed there.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), General Section A

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Four - Your Duties if Injury Occurs
q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, when an injury occurs that may be covered, the employer must tell the insurer:
choices: Only after the employee files a claim
explain: Part Four requires the employer to tell the insurer at once if an injury occurs that may be covered by the policy. Its other duties include providing immediate medical and other services required by the workers compensation law and promptly giving the insurer all notices, demands and legal papers related to the injury.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Four

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Four - Your Duties if Injury Occurs
q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the employer's duties when an injury occurs include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Provide for immediate medical services required by the workers compensation law
Give the insurer the names and addresses of the injured person and witnesses
Voluntarily make payments to the injured employee at the insurer's expense
Do nothing after the injury that would interfere with the insurer's right to recover from others
explain: Part Four requires the employer to provide immediate medical and other services required by law, give names and addresses of injured persons and witnesses, promptly forward notices and legal papers, cooperate, and do nothing to interfere with the insurer's right to recover from others. It also states that the employer must not voluntarily make payments, assume obligations or incur expenses, except at its own cost.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Four, items 1-6

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Five - Premium
q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the premium shown on the Information Page at the start of the policy is:
choices: A deposit that is refunded in full when the policy expires
A flat charge based on the number of employees on payroll
The final premium, which is fixed for the entire policy term
An estimate; the final premium is set after the policy ends
explain: Part Five E states that the premium shown on the Information Page, schedules and endorsements is an estimate. The final premium is determined after the policy ends using the actual premium basis (most commonly payroll), with information developed by audit; the employer pays any balance or receives a refund, subject to the minimum premium.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Five C, E and G

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Five - Premium
q: Under the 2015 edition of the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the insurer may audit the employer's records during the policy period and within how long after it ends?
explain: Part Five G of the 2015 edition lets the insurer examine and audit the employer's records during regular business hours during the policy period and within three years after the policy period ends. Information developed by audit is used to determine final premium.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Five G; same text in the copy of WC 00 00 00 C reproduced in the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (Ed. 09/26)

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Five - Premium
q: An employer cancels its Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy in the middle of the term. Under the policy, unless the insurer's manuals provide otherwise, the final premium will be:
choices: Pro rata for the time the policy was in force
More than pro rata, using the insurer's short-rate table
The full estimated annual premium on the Information Page
explain: Part Five E provides that if the employer cancels, final premium is more than pro rata: it is based on the time the policy was in force, increased by the insurer's short-rate cancelation table, and is not less than the minimum premium. If the insurer cancels, final premium is pro rata; manuals can vary the rule (Michigan's Placement Facility, for example, uses pro rata when the insured cancels because it sold the business or no longer has employees).
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Five E; Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (Ed. 09/26), Rule Ten C-D

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Six - Conditions
q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, the insurer's inspections of the employer's workplaces:
choices: Must be made at least once each policy year
Relate only to insurability and the premiums to be charged
Certify that the workplaces comply with safety laws
Make the insurer responsible for the safety of the employees
explain: Part Six A gives the insurer the right, but not the obligation, to inspect at any time and states that its inspections are not safety inspections; they relate only to the insurability of the workplaces and the premiums to be charged. The insurer does not undertake the duty to provide for employee or public safety and does not warrant that the workplaces are safe or comply with laws.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Six A

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Six - Conditions
q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, an insurer must file notice of a workers' compensation policy cancellation with the Workers' Disability Compensation Agency at least how many days before the cancellation takes effect?
explain: Section 621(4)(g) requires every workers' compensation policy in Michigan to contain this provision, and the Michigan Law Endorsement carries it: the insurer must file notice with the agency at least 20 days before a termination or cancellation takes effect, and the termination is not effective as to the employees until 20 days after the agency receives the notice. This is in addition to the policy's own requirement of at least 10 days' advance written notice to the employer.
source: MCL 418.621(4)(g); Michigan Law Endorsement WC 21 03 04, item g, and Rule Ten A, as reproduced in the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (Ed. 09/26); NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Six D.2; agency name per compiler's notes to MCL 418.201 (E.R.O. 2019-3, MCL 125.1998)

sub: WC & EL Policy > Part Six - Conditions
q: Under the Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability Insurance Policy, if a cancellation provision of the policy conflicts with a law that controls cancellation:
choices: The insurer may choose which of the two rules applies
The provision is changed to comply with the law
The policy is void from its inception
explain: Part Six D.4 states that any cancelation provision that conflicts with a law controlling cancelation of the insurance is changed by that statement to comply with the law. In Michigan, for example, state law adds a 20-day notice filing with the Workers' Disability Compensation Agency to the policy's 10-day notice to the employer.
source: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Part Six D.2 and D.4; MCL 418.621(4)(g)

q: Under the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility's rating rules, premium discount recognizes that:
choices: Larger premium policies cost relatively less to issue and service
Employers with better-than-average loss experience should pay less
Employers that prepay the annual premium reduce collection costs
Employers with formal safety programs tend to have fewer injuries
explain: Rule Seven of the Placement Facility manual states that premium discount recognizes that the relative expense of issuing and servicing larger premium policies is less than for small premium policies. Adjusting premium for an employer's own loss experience is the job of the experience modification, not premium discount.
source: Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (2026 edition, Ed. 09/26), Part One, Rule Seven A; Rule Six G and I

q: In the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility's premium calculation, premium discount is applied to:
choices: Standard premium, after the experience modification
Manual premium, before the experience modification
Premium that is subject to a retrospective rating plan
explain: The Facility's premium algorithm applies the experience modification to reach total standard premium and then subtracts premium discount as a percentage of standard premium. Premium subject to retrospective rating and the expense constant are not subject to premium discount, and the discount applies only when total standard premium exceeds $10,000.
source: Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility Basic Manual (2026 edition, Ed. 09/26), Part One, Rule Six D.3 and I (Michigan Premium Algorithm and arithmetic example), Rule Seven C-D

sub: Other Sources > Self-Insured Employers and Groups (418.611)
q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, an employer that does not insure with an authorized workers' compensation insurer must secure the payment of compensation by:
choices: Buying coverage from an unauthorized surplus lines insurer
Having each employee sign a waiver of benefits
Paying benefits from operating funds without state approval
Receiving authorization to be a self-insurer
explain: Section 611(1) allows only two methods: authorization from the director (now of the Workers' Disability Compensation Agency) to be a self-insurer, granted on a showing of solvency and financial ability to pay, or insurance with an insurer authorized to write workers' compensation in Michigan. An employee's agreement to waive compensation is not valid (the only exception is an election made after injury under Section 161).
source: MCL 418.611(1); MCL 418.815; MCL 418.201 and compiler's notes (E.R.O. 2003-1; E.R.O. 2019-3)

q: Under the Michigan Worker's Disability Compensation Act, 2 or more private employers in the same industry may be permitted to pool their liabilities as a self-insurer group if their combined assets are at least:
explain: Section 611(2) lets the director permit 2 or more employers in the same industry with combined assets of $1,000,000 or more, or 2 or more public employers of the same type of unit, to pool their liabilities to qualify as self-insurers. Each private employer member must agree in writing to be jointly and severally liable for lawful awards against any member of the group.
